svg.title: The integral cusp: strict and elementary standardness
svg.desc: Inverting t squared in Z[t squared,t cubed] gives the standard smooth Laurent ring. Every elementary-standard power would force a differential du from the cusp algebra to be a basis, which is impossible by the Laurent unit calculation. A linear combination of the two Jacobian minors still makes every power at least three strictly standard.
svg.text: The integral cusp: strict and elementary standardness
A = Z[t²,t³] = Z[X,Y]/(Y² − X³); a = t²
A[1/a] = B = Z[t,t⁻¹] = Z[T,V]/(TV − 1): standard smooth
Ω(B/Z) = B dt; B units = { ±tᵏ : k integer }
u = c₀ + Σ(n≥2) cₙ tⁿ ⇒ du = (Σ(n≥2) n cₙ tⁿ⁻¹) dt
n cₙ cannot be ±1 for n ≥ 2; no du from A is a basis.
An elementary-standard power in ANY presentation
⇒ one unselected coordinate u in A has du a basis ⇒ contradiction.
Strict standardness: the two minors are −3X² and 2Y.
Every aᵉ, e ≥ 3, is strictly standard; no positive power is elementary standard.
